experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis is feasible given the available datasets and compute constraints. We use the AG News dataset, which provides sufficient labeled examples for both high-resource (English) and low-resource simulation (by subsampling). The experiment simulates low-resource conditions by training on 10% of the in-language data, which is well within the compute budget of a few hours on a shared GPU node. The sparse fine-tuning method is reused from literature (Composable Sparse Fine-Tuning) and is compatible with standard HuggingFace transformers.
experiment_plans.objective: To test whether sparse fine-tuning on multilingual pretrained language models (mPLMs) enables effective cross-lingual sentiment classification in low-resource languages with as little as 10% of the in-language training data required by full fine-tuning, while maintaining performance comparable to full fine-tuning on high-resource languages.
experiment_plans.design: Controlled comparative experiment with two groups: full fine-tuning and sparse fine-tuning. For each group, we train on 10% of the training data (simulating low-resource condition) and evaluate performance on the test set. Performance is compared against full fine-tuning on 100% of the data (high-resource baseline).

data_requirements.description: The AG News dataset contains 120,000 short news articles across 4 categories (World, Sports, Business, Sci/Tech). It is used to simulate a high-resource language setting where full fine-tuning is possible. The dataset is already on disk and provides sufficient labeled examples for both training and testing.
preprocessing_steps: Filter the data to keep only the 'Business' category to simulate a binary sentiment classification task (positive/negative)
Convert labels to binary (0 for negative, 1 for positive) based on the category
Split the filtered data into 10% and 100% subsets for training
Use the test set from ag_news_document_text_category_classification_test.csv for evaluation

methods.name: Multilingual pretrained language models (mPLMs)
methods.description: We use a multilingual pretrained language model (mBERT) as the base model for cross-lingual transfer. The model is initialized with pre-trained weights and fine-tuned on the AG News dataset to classify sentiment. This method is reused from literature and is suitable for zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual transfer.

methods.name: Composable Sparse Fine-Tuning
methods.description: We apply sparse fine-tuning techniques to update only a small subset of model parameters during training. This method is reused from literature and aims to reduce the need for large in-language training datasets by focusing on key parameters that contribute most to performance.

evaluation.baseline: Full fine-tuning on 100% of the training data
evaluation.success_criteria: If sparse fine-tuning achieves performance (accuracy and F1-score) comparable to full fine-tuning on 100% of the data when trained on only 10% of the data, the hypothesis is supported. If sparse fine-tuning performs significantly worse than full fine-tuning on 100% of the data, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Load the AG News training dataset (ag_news_document_text_category_classification_train.csv) and filter for 'Business' category to create a binary sentiment classification task. Split the data into 10% and 100% subsets for training.
Initialize a multilingual BERT (mBERT) model for sequence classification using HuggingFace Transformers. Set up the tokenizer and model configuration for binary sentiment classification.
Train the mBERT model using full fine-tuning on 100% of the training data. Save the trained model as a baseline.
Train the mBERT model using sparse fine-tuning on 10% of the training data. Apply the Composable Sparse Fine-Tuning technique to update only a subset of parameters.
Evaluate both models (full fine-tuned and sparse fine-tuned) on the test set (ag_news_document_text_category_classification_test.csv) using accuracy and F1-score metrics.
Compare the performance of the sparse fine-tuned model against the full fine-tuned model on the test set. Record the results for analysis.

risks: Insufficient performance difference between full and sparse fine-tuning to draw meaningful conclusions
Overfitting on the small 10% subset leading to inflated performance estimates
Computational cost exceeding the allocated time for training on a single GPU node
